strengths: Originality: The filtering-and-refinement combination of a zero-cost proxy, regularized evolution, and successive halving is a sensible approach to budget-aware NAS, and focusing on tabular architectures is comparatively underexplored.

Significance: NAS-Bench-Tabular could be a useful community resource. It evaluates up to 160,000 fixed-depth MLP width configurations on Frappe and Diabetes, plus 10,000 configurations on Criteo, and records validation performance and training cost.

Soundness: ExpressFlow exhibits strong Spearman correlations with validation AUC on the studied spaces (0.82, 0.73, and 0.90), outperforming nine reported zero-cost proxies. Ablations examine positivity, initialization, batch size, and the proposed width/depth recalibration.

Evaluation breadth: The paper includes comparisons with TabNAS, regularized-evolution NAS, warm-up and move-proposal combinations, a weight-sharing baseline, and multiple search budgets. Several search-strategy experiments are repeated 100 times.

Presentation: The high-level motivation and two-phase pipeline are understandable, and the appendix contains dataset statistics, training hyperparameters, pseudocode, sensitivity studies, and compute hardware.
weaknesses: Soundness—the central "anytime" claim is not established. ATLAS requires a predefined final budget to choose M and K, then runs filtering before refinement. The paper gives no mechanism for returning a trained incumbent when interrupted during filtering or for continuing rather than restarting when the budget is extended. Figure 6 appears to evaluate independent budget-specific runs, and its ATLAS curves are not strictly monotone despite the text claiming equal-or-better results as the budget increases.

The purported coordinator is largely an empirically tuned heuristic, not the stated joint optimization. Equation 2 defines the unknown performance p through ATLAS itself and supplies no solvable performance model or selection rule. The operational choices M/K≈30 and U=2 are selected on the same three benchmark datasets used for evaluation, without held-out datasets or an out-of-distribution test of the coordinator.

The theoretical justification for ExpressFlow does not support the claimed characterization of both trainability and expressivity. The appendix only rewrites neuron saliency as grouped synaptic saliencies; it proves neither correlation with trained performance nor an expressivity result. The trajectory-length factor is not operationally defined, and the appendix's final score derivation omits the K_l/ell(z_l) recalibration used in Equation 1. Equation 11 also appears to replicate the bias contribution inside a sum over incoming units.

The evidence has limited external validity. All tabular experiments use four-layer ReLU MLPs and vary only layer widths, on just three binary-classification datasets. ExpressFlow and the coordinator are developed and assessed on these same exhaustive tables. This does not substantiate broad claims about tabular NAS, other depths/operators, regression or multiclass tasks, or modern tabular architectures.

Benchmark reliability is insufficiently documented. The manuscript does not clearly report multiple independent training seeds per architecture, uncertainty in stored architecture performance, exact train/validation/test splits, preprocessing, or whether final claims use a held-out test set. AUC differences are often only a few 1e-4, so training noise could materially change architecture rankings and reported global optima.

The runtime comparison is under-specified. Figure 6 does not clearly state repetitions or numerical uncertainty, and the 82.75x headline depends on reaching a single benchmark-defined optimum. The cost model ignores coordination and construction overhead, uses architecture-independent t1 and t2, and is ambiguous about whether successive-halving training resumes or restarts. It also mishandles edge cases such as K=1, for which floor(log_eta K)=0 assigns zero refinement cost.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: Appendix I says code and data are available at a URL, but the URL is blank. The pseudocode omits important implementation details, the total compute used to construct the benchmark is not reported, and several checklist answers—such as complete proofs, limitations, and all training details—are not supported by the manuscript.

Presentation and limitations: The paper is readable at a high level but contains inconsistent notation (M versus N in Figure 18, repeated definitions of N, trajectory indices, and an undefined practical computation of trajectory length), grammatical issues, and overstatements such as calling the restricted width-only space "comprehensive." It contains no substantive limitations section despite claiming one in the checklist.

Ethics: The Diabetes benchmark contains sensitive clinical encounters and attributes such as race, gender, and age, yet consent, personally identifiable information, and societal impacts are all marked N/A. Even for an existing public dataset, provenance, licensing, privacy safeguards, subgroup risks, and potential harms of architecture selection for healthcare prediction warrant discussion.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly motivated and generally well organized. It defines the filtering, refinement, and coordination components separately and provides substantial supplementary material. The exhaustive evaluation of many MLP width configurations could become a useful NAS resource. The paper also reports architecture statistics, training hyperparameters, hardware, and comparisons among several search strategies and zero-cost proxies.

ExpressFlow achieves strong Spearman correlations on all three studied datasets (0.82, 0.73, and 0.90 in Table 1), and the appendix includes useful ablations of initialization, batch size, parameter positivity, and recalibration weights.

The practical combination of inexpensive filtering and successive-halving refinement is intuitive and potentially useful under a fixed compute budget. The reported speedups are large on Frappe and Criteo.

The empirical scope goes beyond the main comparison: the paper examines training-free/training-based combinations, a weight-sharing baseline, sensitivity to coordinator parameters, and transfer of ExpressFlow to image NAS benchmarks.
weaknesses: Soundness: ATLAS does not convincingly meet the standard definition of an anytime algorithm. It requires Tmax in advance and chooses M and K specifically for that budget, making it a budget-aware contract algorithm. Results at different budgets appear to come from separately configured runs; median performance across such runs does not show that one uninterrupted run can be stopped at arbitrary times or that its incumbent improves monotonically. This undermines the central “anytime NAS” claim.

Soundness: the claimed “joint optimization” is not actually specified. Equation 2 writes an unknown final performance p as the objective but supplies no model or algorithm for optimizing it. The coordinator instead fixes U=2 and M/K≈30 from empirical sensitivity studies on the same three benchmark datasets. There is no validation that this rule generalizes to unseen datasets, search spaces, hardware, or time regimes.

Soundness: the theoretical account of ExpressFlow does not establish the claimed characterization of both trainability and expressivity. Appendix G.3 mostly rewrites neuron saliency in terms of synaptic saliency; it provides no theorem connecting the score to trained performance or expressivity and omits the proposed trajectory-length recalibration from the analysis. Moreover, Equation 12 incorrectly moves an absolute value outside sums, replacing a sum of absolute neuron terms by the absolute value of a global sum. Thus the checklist's claim of complete theoretical proofs is not supported.

Evaluation: all architecture selection and headline results use validation AUC, with no held-out test performance reported. Data splits are not specified, despite the checklist claiming that they are. If each architecture is trained only once, the declared “global best” can also reflect optimization noise and multiple-comparison bias rather than a robust optimum.

Evaluation: evidence is restricted to three binary-classification datasets and a narrow search space consisting only of four-layer MLPs with variable widths. Criteo contains only 10,000 configurations rather than the 160,000 used for Frappe and Diabetes. These choices substantially limit the significance of broad claims about tabular NAS and transfer to other architectures or tasks.

Evaluation: the timing comparison is insufficiently controlled. The paper reports an eight-RTX-3090 machine and notes that refinement can run in parallel, but it does not clearly state per-method GPU allocation, whether reported costs are wall-clock time or aggregate compute, or whether benchmark lookups and real training are mixed. Figure 6 lacks a precise protocol, run count, and explanation of its uncertainty bands. Consequently, the headline 82.75x speedup is not independently interpretable.

Originality and significance: filtering candidates with a zero-cost proxy and refining them through successive halving is a natural composition of established components—regularized evolution, saliency proxies, and successive halving. ExpressFlow is closely related to SynFlow/synaptic saliency with neuron-wise aggregation and heuristic width/depth weighting. The paper does not provide sufficiently strong theoretical or out-of-domain empirical evidence to elevate this combination into a major methodological contribution.

Reproducibility: Appendix I says that code, data, and instructions are available at a URL, but the URL is blank in the submitted manuscript. Random seeds, dataset splits, preprocessing, repeated-training policy for benchmark entries, detailed baseline tuning, and coordinator implementation are missing or unclear. This conflicts with several affirmative answers in the reproducibility checklist and prevents reliable reconstruction of the main claims.

Presentation and limitations: the high-level exposition is readable, but important definitions are operationally incomplete—notably how trajectory length is computed—and there are notation/indexing errors and typos such as “refinemnet.” The manuscript claims to discuss limitations in its checklist, yet no substantive limitations discussion is present.

Ethics: marking societal impact, consent, and personally identifiable information as N/A is not adequate given the use of longitudinal hospital records with demographic attributes and advertising/user-interaction data. Even if the public datasets are deidentified, the paper should discuss dataset licenses, privacy status, demographic bias, and the risks of interpreting validation gains as support for healthcare deployment.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a useful, underexplored problem—time-budget-aware NAS for tabular models—and combines zero-cost filtering with successive-halving refinement in an intuitive, practically relevant framework.

Soundness: ExpressFlow is evaluated against nine zero-cost proxies and attains the best Spearman correlation on all three datasets (0.82, 0.73, and 0.90). The paper also includes useful ablations of initialization, batch size, positivity, and saliency recalibration.

Evaluation breadth: The experiments compare against several training-based search strategies, TabNAS, alternative combinations of training-free and training-based evaluation, and a weight-sharing baseline. The reported search-time improvements are substantial within the constructed benchmark.

Resource contribution: NAS-Bench-Tabular records training and validation statistics for a large number of width configurations, which could facilitate inexpensive controlled NAS experiments if fully released and documented.

Presentation: The filtering/refinement decomposition is easy to understand, the manuscript is generally well organized, and the appendices provide pseudocode, hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, computational resources, and additional sensitivity analyses.
weaknesses: The central anytime claim is not established. ATLAS is configured for a predefined Tmax, whereas a true anytime algorithm should support interruption or extension of one continuing run. The manuscript does not explain how a run configured for one budget is resumed when additional budget arrives, and monotonic improvement is shown only empirically, not guaranteed for individual stochastic runs.

The claimed strict budget guarantee relies on an approximate cost model: T1=t1M and T2=KUt2 floor(log_eta K). It treats scoring and per-epoch training times as constants despite architecture-dependent widths, omits construction, coordination, and communication overhead, and is inconsistent with the discussion of parallel execution. Consequently, completing within every wall-clock budget is not mathematically ensured.

The evaluation uses validation AUC as both the search objective and final reported performance. No held-out test performance of selected architectures is reported. Moreover, M/K≈30 and U=2 are selected using the same small collection of datasets on which ATLAS is evaluated, leaving open benchmark-level overfitting and generalization to unseen datasets.

Scope is limited to three binary-classification datasets and a fixed four-layer MLP search space varying only layer widths; Criteo has only 10,000 candidates. This is much narrower than the broad claims about tabular NAS, and comparisons with simple size/topology heuristics would be important because ExpressFlow is strongly affected by width and Figure 3 visibly shows size-performance structure.

The theoretical discussion does not substantiate its strongest interpretation. Rewriting neuron saliency in terms of synaptic saliency does not prove that ExpressFlow measures either expressivity or trainability or predicts final generalization. There are also technical inconsistencies: Leaky ReLU is incorrectly said to have nonnegative activations, the positivity argument ignores the stated batch-normalization layers, the trajectory-length factor is not operationally defined, and Equation 11 appears to duplicate the bias contribution over input indices.

Statistical reporting is insufficient. Although some plots contain bands and Figure 4 mentions 100 runs, the meaning of the bands, run counts for the main anytime comparison, seed protocol, and uncertainty for speedup and target-hitting-time claims are not clearly stated. The benchmark also appears to retain one training outcome per architecture, so training noise is not characterized despite the checklist claiming error bars are reported.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: Appendix I says code and data are available at a URL, but the URL is blank in the supplied manuscript. Data splits and preprocessing are also underspecified. The appendix checklist's affirmative claims about code, limitations, licenses, and complete proofs are not supported by the visible paper.

Limitations and ethics receive inadequate treatment. There is no substantive limitations section despite the checklist answer, and marking societal impact, consent, and personally identifiable information as not applicable is too cursory for a benchmark containing historical clinical encounters. At minimum, de-identification, access conditions, licensing, and risks of model selection for healthcare data should be discussed.
